country: United States (Texas: Cameron, El Paso, Hidalgo, and Webb border counties)

evidence_quotes.quote: Where the law does not mandate universal service, poor communities frequently are omitted from drinking water supply networks.
The analysis reveals that rate regulation, intended to make water service affordable to all households, is also responsible, and may actually reduce service coverage among the poor.
Rates not regulated, although rates and connection costs can be appealed to TCEQ.
Thus, relying on a price-regulated supplier to provide service reduces the likelihood of having obtained service through 1996 by 27%. The effect is estimated very precisely.
Providers' access to this infrastructure subsidy has no statistically significant effect

headline_result_summary: In a cross-sectional probit analysis of 781 low-income Texas border colonias as of 1996, water rate regulation (in the absence of a universal service mandate) significantly reduces household access to centralized drinking water networks: colonias located in or near the service territory of a price-regulated public supplier (municipalities, counties, or general law water districts) are 27.2 percentage points less likely to have acquired central water service than colonias served by rate-unregulated providers—primarily non-profit member-owned water supply corporations (WSCs) and small private for-profit suppliers (Model B pricereg probit coefficient = -1.1858, SE = 0.4163, p = 0.004, marginal effect = -0.2718). Descriptive comparisons confirm this is not due to cream-skimming, as WSCs connect 95.1% of nearby colonias despite serving smaller, poorer, and more rural colonias than municipalities (59.0% served) or counties/districts (64.6% served). By contrast, supplier eligibility for generous USDA Rural Development infrastructure grants and low-interest loans has no statistically significant effect on coverage (rurald probit coefficient = 0.2162, p = 0.401). At the county governance level, lax enforcement of state Model Subdivision Rules (violmsr) is strongly negatively associated with water coverage (-40.2 to -69.4 percentage points, p <= 0.004), whereas months of delay in adopting the rules (datemsr) is null.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. Orientation of rate regulation vs. deregulation: The focal exposure in Model B is price regulation (pricereg = 1 for regulated public providers vs. 0 for unregulated WSCs and for-profits), which has a negative sign (-27.2 percentage points, p = 0.004) on physical network coverage (water96). Rate regulation is therefore UNFAVORABLE to water service coverage in the absence of a universal service mandate; if a coder reframes the exposure as 'pricing flexibility' or 'rate deregulation,' the sign and valence invert to positive / favorable to access. Do not confuse the coverage outcome (water96) with water tariffs/affordability (no household tariff regressions are estimated). 2. Inverse coding and county-saturation of violmsr: violmsr = 1 denotes county VIOLATION / lax enforcement of Model Subdivision Rules (Hidalgo County only), so its negative coefficient (-4.6080 in Model A; -7.5722, ME = -0.6943 in Model B) means stronger regulatory enforcement is favorable to access. However, because the sample spans only 4 counties and includes 3 county-level regressors (percent, datemsr, violmsr), the county-level covariates fully saturate cross-county variation (note in unadjusted Table 1, Hidalgo County actually has only 11.9% unserved—the highest raw coverage—before controlling for colonia population share and WSC prevalence). 3. Endogenous baseline in Model A (providr5): Colonias hire private for-profit suppliers (2% of sample) specifically to obtain service, making providr5 a mechanical reference group rather than a causal test of for-profit privatization; also note providr2 (municipal) has p = 0.051 (just above strict 0.05, though described by the author as significant at 95%). 4. Sample selection note: Text p. 139 cites 81% water coverage (matching Table 1 population figures), while Table 3 reports mean water96 = 0.86 in the N = 781 merged regression sample due to missing OAG demographic data for smaller, less-served colonias.
study_design: Cross-sectional observational econometric study (multivariate probit regressions with heteroskedasticity- and geographic-cluster-robust standard errors)
unit_and_sample_size: Unincorporated border subdivisions (colonias); N = 781 colonias across 4 Texas border counties (total colonia population in sample counties = 267,384 in 1996; sample colonia mean population = 264, range 4 to 5,200)
